the effects of TMT on the acquisition and extinction of appetitive behavior in the adult rat.
the effects of acute exposure to the organometallic compound trimethyltin (TMT), a neurotoxin that selectively damages the hippocampus.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
TMT-induced hippocampus damage impairs appetitive acquisition and retention of both CRF and PRF training and that the PRF extinction effect is preserved.
TMT-treated rats exhibit deficits in both acquisition and extinction performance.
TMT-induced hippocampus lesions are not associated with deficits in appetitive learning and memory.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
TMT-treated rats exhibit a general impairment of learning and memory that is not specific to a particular task or to the hippocampal system.

TMT-treated animals exhibit a pattern of behavioral impairment that is similar to that seen in animals with hippocampal lesions and that the pattern of impairment is not dependent on the dose regimen used.

TMT-induced lesions produce deficits in appetitive learning and memory, and that the deficits are not restricted to the acquisition and retention of information, but extend to processes involved in the extinction of learned responses.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the behavioral effects of TMT-induced hippocampectomy in the adult rat are not limited to learning and memory impairments.
TMT-induced hippocampus lesions are not a necessary and sufficient condition to account for the behavioral deficits observed in TMT-treated animals.
TMT is an excellent neurotoxin for studying the role of hippocampus in learning and memory.
